The proposed answer is not the maximum: it is far smaller than an achievable value.

**Upper bound.** Condition 2 forces P to contain at most one set from each complementary pair {A, S∖A}. Applying condition 2 to A and A′ gives A∩A′ ≠ ∅ for every A in P. If A′ = S∖A, then A∩A′ = ∅, so such a set cannot be in P. These are the sets that contain exactly one element from each of the 500 pairs {i, 1001−i}, and there are 2^500 of them. They form complementary pairs among themselves, so at most (2^1000 − 2^500)/2 = 2^999 − 2^499 sets can lie in P.

**Construction.** Take all sets with more than 500 elements. Two such sets must intersect, and the map A ↦ A′ preserves size. For the 500-element sets, two of them are disjoint only if they are complements. So any choice of one set from each complementary pair works, provided P is closed under ′ and excludes the 2^500 bad sets. The orbits of {identity, complement, ′, complement∘′} allow such a choice, so the bound 2^999 − 2^499 is achieved.

The maximum is therefore 2^999 − 2^499. The proposed answer restricts the 500-element sets to those containing one fixed pair, which gives only C(998,498) of them. That is far fewer than the roughly C(1000,500)/2 − 2^499 available, so the proposed value is too small.

VERDICT: REJECT
